content: Plantar fasciitis is a common musculoskeletal condition characterized by inflammation or microtears of the plantar fascia, a thick band of connective tissue supporting the arch of the foot. It typically causes localized heel pain, especially during the first steps after rest or in the morning. The plantar fascia functions to absorb shock and maintain the structural integrity of the foot during walking and standing. Repetitive strain, overuse, or biomechanical abnormalities lead to microscopic damage and inflammation. Its major synonyms include plantar heel pain and plantar fasciopathy. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical history and physical examination, sometimes aided by imaging. Management primarily involves conservative measures such as rest, stretching exercises, orthotic support, and anti-inflammatory therapies. Surgery is seldom needed and reserved for refractory cases. While most respond well to treatment, some cases can become chronic with significant functional impairment. Lifestyle factors such as obesity, occupational standing, and inappropriate footwear contribute to risk. Misconceptions include confusing plantar fasciitis with heel spurs or systemic inflammatory diseases. Safety considerations include avoiding harmful repetitive impact during healing and cautious use of corticosteroid injections due to reported risks. Limitations in current evidence include variability in treatment effectiveness and lack of strong data on some interventions such as shockwave therapy. Summarily, plantar fasciitis is an important condition affecting foot health, with well-established clinical features and evidence-based management approaches, warranting appropriate recognition and patient education.

chunk_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Plantar Fascia
content: The plantar fascia is a thick fibrous aponeurosis that originates from the medial tubercle of the calcaneus (heel bone) and fans out across the sole of the foot to the base of the toes. It supports the arch of the foot, absorbs mechanical shock, and plays a key role in foot biomechanics during gait. The tissue is primarily composed of collagen fibers and is classified as dense regular connective tissue. Dysfunction or microscopic injury to this structure can cause plantar fasciitis.

chunk_title: Definition and Clinical Features of Plantar Fasciitis
content: Plantar fasciitis is defined as inflammation or microtearing of the plantar fascia, leading to localized heel pain that is most notable during initial weight-bearing after rest, especially in the morning or after prolonged sitting. Pain typically decreases with activity but may worsen with prolonged standing or walking later. Clinically, tenderness is palpable at the plantar aspect of the heel near the medial calcaneal tubercle.

chunk_title: Causes and Mechanisms of Plantar Fasciitis
content: The primary mechanism involves repetitive microtrauma and overload of the plantar fascia exceeding its capacity for repair. Risk factors include sudden increases in physical activity, biomechanics abnormalities such as flat feet or high arches, obesity, prolonged standing or walking on hard surfaces, and tight calf muscles. This leads to collagen degeneration, partial tearing, and inflammation within the fascia.

content: Plantar fasciitis affects approximately 10% of the population at some point, most commonly adults between 40 and 60 years. Women are slightly more affected than men. Risk factors include obesity, occupations requiring extensive standing or walking, athletic activities like running, biomechanical foot irregularities, and age-related degenerative changes. Limited ankle dorsiflexion and tight Achilles tendons also contribute to risk.

The pain typically improves as the fascia warms up but may return after prolonged exertion. Other symptoms may include stiffness and mild swelling but rarely redness or systemic signs.

content: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and physical examination. Palpation reveals tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle. Imaging such as ultrasound or MRI may be used to assess fascia thickness or rule out other pathologies but are typically unnecessary. Heel spurs may be seen on X-ray but are not diagnostic or causative of plantar fasciitis.

content: Initial management focuses on rest and modification of activities to reduce fascia strain. Stretching exercises targeting the plantar fascia and calf muscles are effective. Use of orthotic devices or heel pads to provide arch support and cushioning can improve symptoms. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may provide pain relief. Physical therapy can incorporate modalities such as ultrasound or taping.

content: For refractory cases, treatments include corticosteroid injections, platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections, extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT), and rarely surgery. Corticosteroids can provide short-term pain relief but carry risks such as fascia rupture. PRP and ESWT have emerging but limited evidence of efficacy. Surgical plantar fascia release is reserved for persistent severe pain unresponsive to conservative measures.

content: Preventative strategies include wearing appropriate footwear with adequate arch support and cushioning, maintaining healthy weight to reduce mechanical load, gradually increasing activity intensity to avoid overuse, performing regular calf and plantar fascia stretching exercises, and avoiding prolonged standing on hard surfaces whenever possible. Proper warm-up before physical activities reduces injury risk.

content: Common misconceptions are that heel spurs cause plantar fasciitis; however, spurs are often incidental and not the source of pain. Another misconception is that plantar fasciitis is simply inflammation; histological studies suggest degenerative changes (fasciosis) predominate. Additionally, many believe surgery is frequently needed, yet over 90% improve with conservative care. Confusing plantar fasciitis with systemic inflammatory diseases like rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect.

content: While plantar fasciitis is generally safe and non-life-threatening, improper treatment or premature return to intense activity may exacerbate symptoms or lead to chronic pain. Repeated corticosteroid injections risk fascia rupture and fat pad atrophy. Surgical interventions carry risks of nerve damage, infection, and prolonged recovery. Early professional evaluation is advised if symptoms persist beyond several months or worsen.
